title: Generalizing Oresme: The Cauchy Condensation Test
description: The Cauchy condensation test completely characterizes convergence/divergence for monotone decreasing nonneg sequences, generalizing Oresme's 14th-century grouping argument for the harmonic series.

overview.historicalContext: Nicole Oresme (~1350) proved the harmonic series diverges by grouping terms: each group of 2^k terms sums to at least 1/2, giving infinitely many groups each contributing at least 1/2. Augustin-Louis Cauchy (1821) generalized this to the condensation test: for any nonneg antitone sequence f, Σ f(n) converges iff Σ 2^k·f(2^k) converges. This completely characterizes convergence for monotone decreasing sequences.
overview.problemStatement:
Can Oresme's grouping argument be generalized to characterize all divergent series with terms decreasing to zero?

**Answer: Yes.** The Cauchy condensation test provides a complete biconditional characterization.
overview.text: The Cauchy condensation test generalizes Oresme's grouping argument to a complete characterization of convergence for monotone decreasing nonneg sequences.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. Wrap Mathlib's `summable_condensed_iff_of_nonneg` as the Cauchy condensation test.
2. Show Oresme's harmonic divergence follows: f(n)=1/n gives condensed series Σ 2^k/2^k = Σ 1, which diverges.
3. Verify concordance with Mathlib's direct `not_summable_one_div_natCast`.
keyInsights: **Oresme = Condensation**: Oresme's grouping is exactly the condensation test for f(n)=1/n. The condensed series Σ 2^k·(1/2^k) = Σ 1 trivially diverges.
**Complete Characterization**: The condensation test is an exact biconditional, not just a sufficient condition. Any nonneg antitone sequence can be tested this way.
**Broad Applications**: Applies to p-series (1/n^p), log-harmonic (1/(n log n)), iterated logarithms, and all other monotone decreasing sequences.
**Simplification Power**: Reduces subtle convergence questions to checking geometric-type series.

sections.title: The Cauchy Condensation Test
sections.summary: States the Cauchy condensation test: Summable f ↔ Summable (2^k · f(2^k)) for nonneg antitone f. Includes contrapositive form for divergence.
sections.mathContext: For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f \geq 0$ and $f$ antitone on positives: $\sum f(n)$ converges $\iff$ $\sum 2^k f(2^k)$ converges.

sections.title: Oresme's Argument as a Special Case
sections.summary: Proves 1/n is nonneg and antitone, shows condensed harmonic = Σ 1 diverges, and derives Oresme's divergence of Σ 1/n via condensation. Verifies concordance with Mathlib.
sections.mathContext: For $f(n) = 1/n$: the condensed series is $\sum 2^k \cdot \frac{1}{2^k} = \sum 1 = \infty$. Therefore $\sum 1/n = \infty$.

sections.title: Complete Characterization
sections.summary: Documents applications (p-series, log-harmonic, iterated log) and restates the characterization as an exact biconditional.
sections.mathContext: The condensation test is a complete characterization: it is both necessary and sufficient for convergence of nonneg antitone sequences. No weaker condition suffices.

conclusion.summary: The Cauchy condensation test completely answers OQ-04: Oresme's grouping argument generalizes to an exact biconditional characterization of convergence for all monotone decreasing nonneg sequences. The formalization wraps Mathlib's condensation test and demonstrates Oresme's result as a special case.
conclusion.implications: Any convergence question about monotone decreasing nonneg sequences reduces to checking the condensed series Σ 2^k·f(2^k), which is typically simpler to analyze.
openQuestions: Can the condensation test be extended to non-monotone sequences with controlled oscillation?
What is the optimal rate of convergence for condensation approximation of partial sums?
